description: Twenty fixed tutor conversations grounded in the approved N2 B002 questions and draft N2 lesson explanations awaiting Mathematics and editorial review.

cases.title: Comparing masses of fruit
cases.learner_message: What two quantities am I comparing, and in which order?
cases.question_title: Comparing masses of fruit

blocks.text: A basket contains 2.4 kg of oranges and 0.8 kg of limes. How many times as great is the mass of the oranges as the mass of the limes?
Compare the two masses by dividing the larger mass by the smaller mass.

lesson_sections.title: Meaning and order of a ratio

blocks.text: A ratio compares quantities in a stated order. In A:B, the first term represents A and the second term represents B. Reversing the order changes the comparison. Quantities should use compatible units before they are compared. A ratio has no unit after the units have been made the same.

When a question asks how many times as much one quantity is as another, divide the first named quantity by the second named quantity. Keep the wording and the order visible while setting up the division.

prompt.text: Write three quarters to five sixths as a ratio with integer terms.

content.text: Use a common multiplier that clears both denominators. The lowest common multiple of 4 and 6 is 12.
Both terms were multiplied by the same positive number, so the ratio remains equivalent.

blocks.text: Equivalent ratios are produced by multiplying or dividing every term by the same non-zero number. If one term changes from 4 to 18, first determine the scale factor 18 divided by 4, then apply that same factor to every corresponding term.
For linked ratios such as A:B and B:C, rewrite both ratios so that the two values representing B are equal. The other terms can then be joined without changing their relative sizes.

Do not subtract quantities when the question asks for a ratio. Do not compare centimetres directly with metres or grams directly with kilograms. Do not apply a scale factor to only one term. Finally, keep the requested order: the ratio of red to blue is not interchangeable with the ratio of blue to red.

cases.title: Simplifying a whole-number ratio
cases.learner_message: I divided only the first term because that was the larger number. Is that valid?
cases.question_title: Simplifying a whole-number ratio

blocks.text: Write 42:63 in its simplest form.
Find the highest common factor of 42 and 63.

lesson_sections.title: Writing a ratio in simplest form

blocks.text: A ratio is in simplest form when its terms are positive integers with no common factor greater than 1. First make units consistent. Then clear decimals or fractions by multiplying every term by a suitable common multiplier. Finally divide every integer term by their greatest common divisor.
For a three-term ratio, the same operation must be applied to all three terms. Checking only adjacent pairs is not enough; find a common divisor of the complete set of terms.

lesson_sections.title: Worked example: simplify a three-term decimal ratio

prompt.text: Write 1.2:1.8:3 in its simplest form.

content.text: Multiply every term by 10 to remove the decimals.
The greatest common divisor of 12, 18 and 30 is 6. Divide every term by 6.
The terms 2, 3 and 5 have no common factor greater than 1, so the ratio is in simplest form.

blocks.text: When ratio terms contain fractions, multiply every term by the lowest common multiple of all denominators. This creates an equivalent integer ratio. Then check whether the resulting integers still share a common factor.
Mixed numbers should first be rewritten as improper fractions. Percentages should be rewritten using a common representation before simplifying.

Do not round decimal terms merely to make them integers. Do not divide different terms by different numbers. Do not stop after clearing fractions or decimals without checking for a remaining common factor. A final ratio such as 0.5:1 is equivalent to 1:2 but is not in the expected positive-integer simplest form.

cases.title: Finding the smaller share of a total
cases.learner_message: I do not understand ratio parts. Can you explain them another way?
cases.question_title: Finding the smaller share of a total

blocks.text: 54 tokens are divided in the ratio 2:7. Find the smaller share.
Add the ratio terms to find the total number of equal parts.

lesson_sections.title: Worked example: share a total in a ratio

prompt.text: A total of 96 tokens is shared in the ratio 3:5. Find the two shares.

content.text: The ratio contains 3 + 5 = 8 equal parts.
One ratio part represents 12 tokens.
Check that the shares add to 96.

lesson_sections.title: Use one ratio part as a unit

blocks.text: In a ratio problem, label what each term represents and count the relevant number of ratio parts. If a total is given, divide the total by the sum of the parts. If one share is given, divide that share by its own number of parts. Use the value of one part to calculate the required quantity.
Always verify whether the stated number is the original total, a remaining total, a difference between shares or one individual share. These correspond to different combinations of ratio parts.

For a before-and-after ratio problem, represent the original quantities with a common multiplier, for example 3k and 5k. Apply additions, removals or transfers to the actual quantities, not to the ratio terms alone. Then use the new ratio or new total to form an equation.
A transfer between two groups preserves the combined total, while an addition or removal changes it. State which invariant you are using before solving.

Label every quantity, preserve the requested order and keep units consistent. After solving, reconstruct the original or changed quantities and check the stated total, difference and ratio. Reject a result that gives a negative count or conflicts with a whole-number requirement in the context.

For a before-and-after ratio problem, represent the original quantities with a common multiplier, for example 3k and 5k. Apply additions, removals or transfers to the actual quantities, not to the ratio terms alone. Then use the new ratio or new total to form an equation.
A transfer between two groups preserves the combined total, while an addition or removal changes it. State which invariant you are using before solving.

Label every quantity, preserve the requested order and keep units consistent. After solving, reconstruct the original or changed quantities and check the stated total, difference and ratio. Reject a result that gives a negative count or conflicts with a whole-number requirement in the context.

cases.title: Combining two rational drink mixtures
cases.learner_message: Demonstrate the method on a simpler mixture with different numbers.
cases.question_title: Combining two rational drink mixtures

blocks.text: Tank P contains 148 litres of a syrup-and-water mixture in the ratio 3/5:1.25. Tank Q contains 144 litres of a syrup-and-water mixture in the ratio 0.84:1.4. All the liquid from both tanks is combined. Find the ratio of syrup to water in the combined mixture, in its simplest form.
Find the syrup and water volumes in each tank separately before combining like quantities.

lesson_sections.title: Meaning and order of a ratio

blocks.text: A ratio compares quantities in a stated order. In A:B, the first term represents A and the second term represents B. Reversing the order changes the comparison. Quantities should use compatible units before they are compared. A ratio has no unit after the units have been made the same.

When a question asks how many times as much one quantity is as another, divide the first named quantity by the second named quantity. Keep the wording and the order visible while setting up the division.

prompt.text: Write three quarters to five sixths as a ratio with integer terms.

content.text: Use a common multiplier that clears both denominators. The lowest common multiple of 4 and 6 is 12.
Both terms were multiplied by the same positive number, so the ratio remains equivalent.

blocks.text: Equivalent ratios are produced by multiplying or dividing every term by the same non-zero number. If one term changes from 4 to 18, first determine the scale factor 18 divided by 4, then apply that same factor to every corresponding term.
For linked ratios such as A:B and B:C, rewrite both ratios so that the two values representing B are equal. The other terms can then be joined without changing their relative sizes.

Do not subtract quantities when the question asks for a ratio. Do not compare centimetres directly with metres or grams directly with kilograms. Do not apply a scale factor to only one term. Finally, keep the requested order: the ratio of red to blue is not interchangeable with the ratio of blue to red.

cases.title: Deducing a common increment from linked ratios
cases.learner_message: The worked solution is unlocked. Explain why the common increment can be represented by one variable.
cases.question_title: Deducing a common increment from linked ratios

blocks.text: Positive quantities p, q and r satisfy p:q = 2:3 and q:r = 4:5. The same positive quantity t is added to p and r, after which (p + t):(r + t) = 3:4. Write p:q:t in its simplest form.
First combine the two overlapping ratios to express p, q and r using one multiplier.

lesson_sections.title: Writing a ratio in simplest form

blocks.text: A ratio is in simplest form when its terms are positive integers with no common factor greater than 1. First make units consistent. Then clear decimals or fractions by multiplying every term by a suitable common multiplier. Finally divide every integer term by their greatest common divisor.
For a three-term ratio, the same operation must be applied to all three terms. Checking only adjacent pairs is not enough; find a common divisor of the complete set of terms.

lesson_sections.title: Worked example: simplify a three-term decimal ratio

prompt.text: Write 1.2:1.8:3 in its simplest form.

content.text: Multiply every term by 10 to remove the decimals.
The greatest common divisor of 12, 18 and 30 is 6. Divide every term by 6.
The terms 2, 3 and 5 have no common factor greater than 1, so the ratio is in simplest form.

blocks.text: When ratio terms contain fractions, multiply every term by the lowest common multiple of all denominators. This creates an equivalent integer ratio. Then check whether the resulting integers still share a common factor.
Mixed numbers should first be rewritten as improper fractions. Percentages should be rewritten using a common representation before simplifying.

Do not round decimal terms merely to make them integers. Do not divide different terms by different numbers. Do not stop after clearing fractions or decimals without checking for a remaining common factor. A final ratio such as 0.5:1 is equivalent to 1:2 but is not in the expected positive-integer simplest form.
